html:
The Menominee are an Algonquian people of northeastern Wisconsin and Michigan's Upper Peninsula, who have lived there longer than any other tribe of the region. Their name, from Ojibwe, means "wild rice people", after the wild rice they harvest from the lakes.

Their land once covered about 10 million acres. They fished, gathered rice, hunted and traded with their neighbours the Ho-Chunk, Ojibwe and Potawatomi, and from the 1600s with New France.

Through treaties in the 1800s they gave up most of their land but refused removal west, and kept a reservation in Wisconsin. They have managed its forest for timber for over a century without depleting it. In the 1950s the US ended its recognition of the tribe. The tribe won the case Menominee Tribe v. United States in 1968 to keep its hunting and fishing rights, and won back recognition in 1973.
